Dukes
dukes
n. pl. (chiefs or clan-heads, in the KJV chiefly of Edom; rendering Hebrew alluph, a chief of a thousand)
From the Latin dux, a leader, through Old French duc. The translators chose the English feudal title to render Hebrew alluph, a tribal chieftain — a leader of a clan or of a thousand, from eleph, a thousand.

Biblical Definition

The dukes of the Authorized Version are chiefly Esau's. Genesis 36 is a long roll of them: “These were dukes of the sons of Esau… duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz” (Genesis 36:15), and the Chronicler repeats the list (1 Chronicles 1:51). The placement is instructive, because Genesis gives Esau a chapter of established chiefs while Jacob's line is still a household of shepherds in a land they do not own. The rejected brother prospers visibly and early. Scripture is unembarrassed by this and does not hurry to correct the impression — it simply keeps telling the story. The Song of the Sea then names them among those who melt: “Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away” (Exodus 15:15). The chiefs who had a chapter to themselves are, one book later, a line in the terror of the nations at what God did at the sea. The word is also used of Midian's chiefs, slain with Balaam: they “were dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country” (Joshua 13:21). Established rank is not, in Scripture, a comment on divine favour.

Webster 1828 Definition

Clan-chiefs, in the KJV chiefly Esau's. Genesis gives the rejected brother a chapter of dukes while Jacob is still landless — and the Song of the Sea shows the same dukes amazed at what God did for the shepherds.

expand to see more

DUKE, n. [Fr. duc; L. dux, a leader, from duco, to lead.] In Great Britain, one of the highest order of nobility; a title of honor next below the princes.

2. In some countries on the continent, a sovereign prince, without the title of king.

3. A chief; a prince; as the dukes of Edom, Gen. 36.

4. DUKEDOM, n. The seignory or possessions of a duke; the territory of a duke.

5. Formerly, a leader or commander of an army.

Key Scripture

Genesis 36:15 — "These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz,"

Exodus 15:15 — "Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away."

1 Chronicles 1:51 — "Hadad died also. And the dukes of Edom were; duke Timnah, duke Aliah, duke Jetheth,"

Joshua 13:21 — "And all the cities of the plain, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, which reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses smote with the princes of Midian, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, which were dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country."

Modern Corruption

Visible rank and early prosperity are read as evidence of divine favour, though Genesis deliberately gives the chiefs and the genealogies to the rejected line while the chosen one waits.

expand to see more

The prosperity teaching that measures God's blessing by present standing has to skip Genesis 36 entirely. Esau, the brother of whom it is written Esau have I hated (Malachi 1:2-3; Romans 9:13), receives a full chapter of dukes, kings, and settled territory, and receives it before Israel has a foot of ground. Asaph felt the difficulty acutely and wrote a psalm about it — he was envious at the foolish when he saw the prosperity of the wicked, until he went into the sanctuary of God, and then understood I their end (Psalm 73:3, 17). Scripture's answer to visible prosperity in the ungodly is not denial but patience about endings.

The principle to recover is the reversal in Exodus 15:15. The dukes of Edom are named there not as powers but as men amazed, and what amazed them was a deliverance granted to slaves. God's election runs on other lines than rank: the younger over the elder, the shepherd over the chief, a nation of brickmakers over a settled aristocracy. Paul draws exactly this conclusion — God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, that no flesh should glory in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:27-29).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew alluph is a chief or clan-head, from eleph, a thousand — the leader of a thousand. It is also used of a familiar friend or guide.

expand to see more

Hebrew alluph (H441) — a chief, a captain of a thousand; the KJV duke in Genesis 36.

Hebrew eleph (H505) — a thousand; the root of the chief's title.

Hebrew nasi (H5387) — a prince, one lifted up; the title of the tribal princes of Israel.

Hebrew rosh (H7218) — a head, chief; the common term for the head of a father's house.

Greek hegemon (G2232) — a leader; the Septuagint term used where the Hebrew has alluph.

Usage

"Of the roll of Esau's chiefs: these were dukes of the sons of Esau (Genesis 36:15)."

"Of those chiefs amazed at the sea: then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed (Exodus 15:15)."

"Of the chiefs of Sihon slain with Midian: which were dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country (Joshua 13:21)."
